title: Single-cell expression and immune infiltration analysis of polyamine metabolism in breast cancer

sections.abstract:
Breast cancer is one of the most threatening women health diseases worldwide and its molecular heterogeneity offers a range of response to therapy. The role of polyamine metabolism is receiving increasing attention. Polyamine metabolism not only plays an important role in the occurrence and development of breast cancer, but also interacts with tumor immune microenvironment. In this work, we applied single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) and systems immunological approaches to interrogate immune cell infiltration gene-to-gene co-expressions in the bulk tumor transcriptomes of breast cancer. We acquired breast cancer sample data from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) and Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO), evaluated the infiltration status of 22 immune cell types using CIBERSORTx tool, respectively. By leveraging the Retrospective Breast sample of various technologies including gene expression and methylation, we identified 46 breast cancer proliferation-associated co-expression modules using weighted gene coexpression network analysis (WGCNA) approach along with machine learning models which in turn delineated single cell level expressions features that these selected module possessed. We observed substantial cellular heterogeneity in the breast cancer microenvironment, where lineage-specific gene expression patterns were highly associated with tumor progression. Moreover, we also identified the gene modules correlated with immune cell infiltration level that could function as regulators in response to tumors for immune therapy. Moreover, risk scores were correlated with immune cell function in different patient groups defined by high- and low-risk. The findings of this study shed a new light upon molecular classification prognostic assessment and personalized treatment in breast cancer.

Keywords: Breast cancer, Single-cell RNA sequencing, Immune microenvironment, Gene co-expression network, Machine learning, Personalized treatment
sections.introduction:
Breast cancer, as one of the most common malignant tumors among women worldwide, has high incidence and mortality rates [ 1 – 3 ]. Despite significant advances in the treatment of breast cancer in recent years, uncertainties still exist in the prognosis due to the heterogeneity of tumors and complex molecular mechanisms. Especially, inflammation and immune cell infiltration within the tumor microenvironment are central to progression, metastasis and treatment response of breast cancer [ 4 – 7 ]. Additionally, polyamine metabolism plays a key role in the biological processes of breast cancer, closely related to cell proliferation, differentiation, and apoptosis [ 8 , 9 ]. Polyamines in the tumor microenvironment, such as spermine, spermidine, and putrescine, not only participate in normal physiological functions of cells but also play important roles in the proliferation, invasion, and metastasis of tumor cells [ 10 ]. Aberrant activation of polyamine metabolism is associated with poor prognosis in breast cancer; therefore, studying the mechanisms of polyamine metabolism in breast cancer is of great significance in discovering new therapeutic targets. Chemotherapy can promote the metabolism of spermidine in breast cancer cells. The active metabolism of spermidine in tumor cells activates anti-tumor immunity, thus promoting tumor immunity.

The emergence of single-cell RNA sequencing technology (scRNA seq) provides an unprecedented high-resolution perspective for studying the complexity and heterogeneity of cells in the tumor microenvironment. This technology can not only reveal the interaction network between tumor cells, immune cells, and other cell types during tumor development, but also further analyze and interpret these data through machine learning algorithms, thereby gaining a deeper understanding of the biological characteristics and potential therapeutic targets of tumors [ 11 – 13 ]. In the research of breast cancer, machine learning analysis of scRNA seq data can identify gene modules related to tumor proliferation and explore their expression characteristics in different cell types. For example, by analyzing the relationship between the level of immune cell infiltration and the risk score of patients, we can reveal how these factors affect the prognosis of breast cancer. In addition, research may also discover the role of polyamine metabolism in breast cancer and its interaction with the immune microenvironment, providing a new perspective for future treatment strategies [ 14 , 15 ]. In addition, converting single-cell sequencing data into image form and combining it with deep learning techniques for cell classification has been proven to significantly improve classification accuracy. This method can more effectively capture complex patterns in data, providing new ideas and effective tools for solving key challenges in single-cell data analysis.

Through these studies, we hope to provide new insights for molecular classification, prognosis evaluation, and individualized treatment of breast cancer, laying the foundation for future clinical research and the development of treatment strategies. We believe that these findings will contribute to advancing the field of breast cancer treatment and bring more effective treatment options to patients.
sections.methods:
The expression matrix and clinical information of breast cancer used in Bulk analysis come from gene expression synthesis (GEO) ( http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/ ) [ 16 ]. The scRNA seq data of breast cancer patients' tissues are from GSM7122852 .The protocol used for the experiment was based on the user guide provided by 10X Genomics for Chromium Next GEM Single Cell 3ʹReagent Kits v3.1. To generate and barcode the GEMs, cells were diluted to achieve approximately 5000 cells per lane and were loaded with the master mix onto the Chromium Next GEM Chip G.

The single-cell WGCNA analysis method mainly includes steps such as data preprocessing, co-expression network construction, module identification and analysis, visualization, and differential analysis [ 17 , 18 ]. Firstly, Seurat package is used for standard preprocessing of the GSM7122852 single-cell dataset, including quality control, normalization, dimensionality reduction, and clustering. Subsequently, the co-expression network is built using WGCNA and hdWGCNA packages to identify gene modules and perform module feature analysis. The steps consist in standardizing choice of soft power thresholds, construction of the network and computation module eigengenes and connectivity measures for differential expression (btw topological overlap), plus identification hub genes. Next, the results are visualized by docking to various visualization tools such as ggplot2 for module dendrogram and UMAP plots. Module-based differential expression analysis and module—trait correlationanalysis are finally performed to unveil the association of modules with biological phenotypes. The complete analysis requires mostly of the popular R packages like Seurat, WGCNA, hdWGCNA to delve through gene co-expression patterns and cellular heterogeneity inside GSM7122852 .

The single-cell WGCNA analysis framework consists of data preprocessing, co-expression network construction and module identification, exploratory and differential expression analyses steps. First of all Seurat package is used to standard preprocessing the GSM7122852 single cell dataset including quality control, normalization, dimensionality reduction and clustering. Then, WGCNA and hdWGCNA packages establish a co-expression network to identify gene modules, as well as perform module feature inspection [ 19 – 21 ]. This includes the definition of soft-power thresholds, building up a network followed by calculation of module eigengenes and connectivity as well as identification hub genes. Then he shows how to visualize the results with visualization tools, like ggplot2 plots of module dendrogram and UMAP. Finally, module differential expression analysis and module-trait correlation analysis are used to analyze the relationship between modules aNd biological phenotypes.

Using a combination of 10 machine learning algorithms and 101 algorithm combinations for machine learning and model construction. The comprehensive algorithms include Random Survival Forest (RSF), Elastic Network (Enet), Lasso, Ridge, Stepwise Cox, CoxBoost, Cox Partial Least Squares Regression (plsRcox), Supervised Principal Component (SuperPC), Generalized Boosting Regression Model (GBM), and Survival Support Vector Machine (survival SVM). Calculate the Harrell correlation index (C-index) for the TCGA and GEO sets, and the model with the highest average C-index is considered the best [ 22 , 23 ].

The calculation formula is as follows: Risk score = ∑ (Coefi × Exp). In this formula, Coefi represents the risk coefficient and Exp represents the expression level. In the training set, samples are divided into high-risk and low-risk clusters based on the median. Then conduct Kaplan Meier survival analysis to compare the OS differences between high-risk and low-risk clusters. Next, use the R package "ggplot2" to perform mapping and draw a Sankey diagram to observe the relationship between two risk clusters and clustering. To further validate, the samples were divided into all, TCGA group, and GEO group for Kaplan Meier survival analysis, ROC curve construction, and DCA analysis.

Independent Student t-test is used to compare continuous data with normal distribution, and chi square discriminant test is used for pairwise comparison between subgroups. Perform Kruskal Wallis test (one-way ANOVA of rankings) to determine if there are statistically significant differences between multiple groups. When the dependent variable is an ordered or continuous variable, but not normally distributed, Mann Whitney U test is used to compare the differences between two independent groups. All statistical analyses were conducted using R programming language (Version 4.0.3). Unless otherwise specified, differences with p < 0.05 indicate statistical significance.
sections.results:
The distribution plot of nFeature_RNA (Fig. 1 A) shows the range of gene counts detected in each cell, with most cells detecting between 1000 and 3000 genes, indicating appropriate sequencing depth and cell quality. The nCount_RNA plot (Fig. 1 B) displays the total RNA counts per cell, typically ranging from 5000 to 20,000 counts. The percentage of mitochondrial genes (Fig. 1 C) is mainly below 25%, indicating a low level of cell stress or death. The scatter plot of gene expression variability (Fig. 1 D) highlights highly variable genes (red dots), which may play a key role in distinguishing cell populations. Weak negative correlation (-0.23) between the percentage of mitochondrial genes and nCount_RNA (Fig. 1 E, F); it is evident SCSCC_13 scRNA-seq has no depleted regions. Principal component analysis (Fig. 1 G) provides insight into the major sources of variation within this data set, with PC_1 and PC_2 representing key biological differences between cells. Figure 1 H Gene expression heatmap showing distinct gene patterns across various cell clusters, giving first insights about the distribution of cells and data quality.

Quality control of breast cancer single cell RNA sequencing data. A NFeature-RNA distribution, B nCount-RNA distribution, C mitochondrial gene percentage, D scatter plot of gene expression variability, E correlation between mitochondrial gene percentage and nCount-RNA, F correlation between nFeature-RNA and nCount-RNA, G. principal component analysis (PCA), H gene expression heatmap

Figure 2 A presents a heatmap of the genes with the highest contributions from the top 15 principal components (PC_1 to PC_15). Each heatmap displays the expression patterns of genes strongly associated with a specific PC in the sample set, with colors ranging from purple to yellow indicating low to high expression levels. Figure 2 B is a Q-Q plot that compares the theoretical quantile and empirical quantile of each PC, with the corresponding p-values listed on the right. PC1 showed the highest statistical significance (p = 2.74e−269), indicating that it captured the most significant source of variation in the dataset. Figure 2 C is a scatter plot showing the standard deviation explained by each PC. The graph shows a sharp decrease in explained variance after the first few PCs. For example, genes in PC_1 (such as TRAC, CD3D, and CXCL13) may be associated with immune responses, while genes in PC_2 (such as COL1A1 and SPARC) may be associated with extracellular matrix remodeling.

The principal component analysis (PCA) results of gene expression data from breast cancer samples. A presents a heatmap of the top genes contributing to the first 15 principal components (PC_1 to PC_15). B is a Q-Q plot, and C is a scatter plot

Figures 3 A, B are UMAP dimensionality reduction visualizations showing the distribution of cell clusters. In Fig. 3 A, cells are labeled by cluster numbers (0–6), while in Fig. 3 B, cells are labeled based on inferred cell types, including fibroblasts, macrophages, proliferating cells, epithelial cells, migrating cells, T cells, and myoepithelial cells. Figures 3 C–F display the parameter optimization process of Weighted Gene Co-expression Network Analysis (WGCNA). Figure 3 C shows the scale-free topology model fit under different soft threshold values, used for choosing the optimal soft threshold. Figures 3 D–F respectively demonstrate the trends of mean connectivity, median connectivity, and maximum connectivity with changing soft threshold values. Figure 3 G is a dendrogram showing the hierarchical clustering results of gene modules obtained from WGCNA analysis, with the colored bars at the bottom representing different gene modules.

The comprehensive analysis results of single-cell RNA sequencing data of breast cancer. A , B are UMAP dimensionality reduction visualization plots, and C – F show the parameter optimization process of Weighted Gene Co-expression Network Analysis (WGCNA). C displays the scale-free topology model fit under different soft thresholds, used to select the optimal soft threshold. D – F respectively show the trends of mean connectivity, median connectivity, and max connectivity with changing soft thresholds. G is a dendrogram

Each subfigure in Fig. 4 represents a gene module (Proliferating-M1 to Proliferating-M46), identified by different colors. The y-axis in each subfigure represents the module membership value (KME, Module Membership) of the genes, reflecting the strength of correlation between the genes and module characteristics. The curves in the figure display the distribution of KME values within each module, with the steepness of the curve indicating the tightness and consistency of the module. The most representative genes in each module are listed on the right side, which may play important roles in the function of proliferating cells. For example, genes such as CENPF, MELK, and CCNB1 in the Proliferating-M1 module are related to the cell cycle and cell division. Genes like HMGB2, PCNA, and RRM2 in the Proliferating-M2 module are associated with DNA replication and repair. Other modules such as Proliferating-M3 (containing genes like VIM, SPARC) may be related to extracellular matrix remodeling and cell migration, while Proliferating-M4 (containing genes like TMEM66, ATP5G1) might involve mitochondrial function and energy metabolism.

Detailed analysis results of 46 co-expression modules of genes in the proliferating cell population of breast cancer. Each subplot represents a gene module (Proliferating-M1 to Proliferating-M46) labeled with different colors. The y-axis of each subplot represents the Module Membership (KME) values of the genes in the module. The curves in the figure display the distribution of KME values for the genes within the module, where the steepness of the curve reflects the tightness and consistency of the module. The most representative genes in each module are listed on the right side of the figure, which may play important roles in the functionality of proliferating cells. Other modules like Proliferating-M3 (containing genes such as VIM, SPARC) may be related to extracellular matrix remodeling and cell migration, while Proliferating-M4 (containing genes like TMEM66, ATP5G1) may involve mitochondrial function and energy metabolism

Each subgraph in Fig. 5 represents a gene module (Proliferating-M1 to Proliferating-M46) visualized using the UMAP dimensional reduction method. In each subgraph, cells are mapped to a two-dimensional space, where the depth of color indicates the average expression level of genes in that module in each cell, with darker colors indicating higher expression levels. The grayscale bar on the right shows the range of expression intensity from low (−) to high ( +). Modules Proliferating-M2 and M3 exhibit different spatial distribution patterns, while some modules (such as Proliferating-M5 and M6) show a relatively uniform expression pattern, possibly representing basic cellular functions that remain active in the majority of proliferating cells. Conversely, other modules (such as Proliferating-M10 and M11) display more limited expression patterns, potentially reflecting specific cell states or functions.

Shows the expression characteristics of 46 co-expression modules of genes in proliferating cell populations of breast cancer at the single-cell level. Each subfigure represents a gene module (Proliferating-M1 to Proliferating-M46), presented using the UMAP dimensional reduction visualization method. In each subfigure, cells are mapped to a two-dimensional space, where the depth of color indicates the average expression level of genes in each cell, with darker colors representing higher expression levels. The grayscale bar on the right displays the range of expression intensity, from low (−) to high ( +). This visualization method reveals the expression patterns and cellular heterogeneity of each module in the proliferating cell population. For example, the Proliferating-M1 module shows high expression in certain cell populations, possibly representing a subpopulation of actively proliferating cells. Proliferating-M2 and M3 modules exhibit different spatial distribution patterns, while other modules (such as Proliferating-M10 and M11) demonstrate more limited expression patterns

Figure 6 A is a heat map showing the correlations between 46 proliferation-related modules, with colors ranging from blue to red indicating negative to positive correlations, revealing functional associations between the modules. Figure 6 B is a UMAP plot illustrating the distribution of different gene modules in two-dimensional space, where each point represents a cell, different colors represent different modules, reflecting the expression characteristics of the modules at the single-cell level. Figure 6 C is a dot plot with the horizontal axis representing 46 modules and the vertical axis representing different cell types (T cells, proliferating cells, myoepithelial cells, migrating cells, macrophages, fibroblasts, and epithelial cells), where the size of the dots indicates the percentage of expression of the module in a specific cell type, and the color represents the average expression level, with colors ranging from blue to red indicating low to high expression. Figure 6 D is a bar plot showing the average log2 fold change of each module, reflecting the level of expression difference of the modules in proliferating cells compared to other cell types. Figure 6 E is a volcano plot with the horizontal axis representing the average log2 fold change and the vertical axis representing −log10(adjusted P-values), where each point represents a module and highlights modules significantly upregulated or downregulated in proliferating cells.

Comprehensively demonstrates the characteristics of gene co-expression modules in proliferating breast cancer cells and their expression patterns in different cell types. Figure 7 A is a set of volcano plots that show the expression changes of gene modules in epithelial cells, fibroblasts, macrophages, migratory cells, myoepithelial cells, proliferating cells, and T cells. Each point represents a module, with the x-axis showing the average log2 fold change and the y-axis showing the -log10 (adjusted P value). Figure 7 B illustrates the expression changes of all modules in proliferating cells relative to other cell types. Figure 7 C is a heatmap showcasing the expression features of 46 gene modules in different cell types. The x-axis represents different modules, and the y-axis represents cell types including all cells, epithelial cells, fibroblasts, macrophages, migratory cells, myoepithelial cells, proliferating cells, and T cells. The colors in the heatmap from blue to red indicate low to high expression levels, with two rows for each cell type representing nFeature_RNA (number of detected genes) and nCount_RNA (total RNA counts). This heatmap effectively displays the expression patterns of each module in different cell types, revealing cell type-specific gene expression characteristics. For instance, certain modules exhibit high expression in specific cell types, such as Proliferating-M10 in proliferating cells.

Comprehensively demonstrates the characteristics of gene expression modules of different cell types in breast cancer and their distribution at the single-cell level. A is a volcano plot. B is a forest plot. C is a heatmap, showing the expression characteristics of 46 gene modules in different cell types

We conducted comparative analysis of multiple algorithms. Figure 8 A shows the AUC values of each model on the training set and validation set ( GSE205185 ), where NaiveBayes, glmBoost + NaiveBayes, and Lasso + NaiveBayes performed well on both datasets. Figure 8 B, C show the confusion matrices of the best-performing models on the training set and GSE205185 dataset, reflecting the accuracy of the models in predicting different categories. Figure 8 D, E further illustrate the performance of the models through ROC curves, with an AUC of 0.996 (95% CI: 0.984–1.000) on the training set and an AUC of 0.847 (95% CI: 0.635–0.988) on the GSE205185 validation set, demonstrating good generalization capability of the model. These results collectively indicate that the machine learning models we developed show promising performance in breast cancer prediction, providing strong support for clinical decision-making.

Performance of Different Machine Learning Models in Breast Cancer Prediction. A : AUC comparison of various machine learning models on the training set and GSE205185 dataset, B : Confusion matrix of the best model on the training set, C : Confusion matrix of the best model on the GSE205185 dataset, D : ROC curve of the best model on the training set, E : ROC curve of the best model on the GSE205185 dataset

We conducted a series of analyses. Figure 9 A shows the differential expression of 20 proteasome-related genes in breast cancer tissues compared to normal tissues, with several genes exhibiting significant differential expression patterns. Figure 9 B visually displays the expression correlations among these genes through a correlation heat map, revealing potential functional interactions. Figure 9 C presents the results of the correlation analysis between proteasome-related genes and various levels of immune cell infiltration, with monocytes showing the most significant negative correlation with the expression of these genes (p = 0.026). Figure 9 D further demonstrates the negative correlation between PSMC4 gene expression and monocyte infiltration levels (R = -0.38, p = 0.026), suggesting that proteasome function may influence breast cancer progression by modulating immune cell infiltration. Finally, Fig. 9 E comprehensively illustrates the interactions between proteasome-related genes and various immune cells through a complex correlation network, offering a holistic view of the role of the proteasome system in the immune microenvironment of breast cancer.

Expression patterns of proteasome-related genes in breast cancer and their relationship with immune cell infiltration. sections.discussion:
This study conducted in-depth analysis of immune cell infiltration and gene co-expression patterns in the breast cancer microenvironment using single-cell RNA sequencing technology and machine learning algorithms. Our research findings not only revealed the complexity of breast cancer cell heterogeneity and immune microenvironment but also provided new insights for molecular classification, prognosis assessment, and personalized treatment of breast cancer.

The role of polyamine metabolism in breast cancer is an active research field. Polyamines, including spermine, spermidine, and putrescine, are important small molecule compounds in cells that play a key role in regulating cell growth, differentiation, apoptosis, as well as DNA and protein synthesis [ 15 , 24 , 25 ]. Here are some potential roles of polyamine metabolism in breast cancer. Polyamines can promote the progression of the cell cycle, especially in the G1 to S phase transition, by binding to nucleic acids and influencing cell proliferation [ 26 , 27 ]. In breast cancer cells, elevated levels of polyamines are associated with enhanced tumor growth and proliferation. Polyamines can inhibit cell apoptosis, possibly by affecting intracellular signaling pathways. Binding of polyamines to DNA helps maintain the stability of DNA structure, but their excessive accumulation may also be related to genomic instability [ 28 , 29 ].

The potential application of polyamine metabolism in the treatment of breast cancer is a research field of great concern. Polyamines are a class of multi cationic alkyl amine metabolites that participate in multiple fundamental biological processes and play important roles in the growth of normal and cancer cells. In breast cancer, the metabolism of polyamines is usually disordered, leading to the increase of polyamines, which makes it a potential target for cancer treatment [ 8 , 30 ]. Iron dependent cell death is a regulatory form of cell death that is triggered by lethal lipid peroxide overload. Research has found that polyamine metabolism exposes the targetable vulnerability of ferroptosis and presents exciting opportunities for cancer treatment [ 31 , 32 ]. Polyamine supplementation induces ferroptosis, making cancer cells or xenografts more sensitive to radiotherapy or chemotherapy.

Our analysis indicated significant cellular heterogeneity in the breast cancer microenvironment, with gene expression patterns of different cell types closely associated with tumor progression. Specifically, we identified unique expression features of gene modules related to tumor proliferation at the single-cell level, potentially linked to the biological behavior of tumor cells and their response to treatment. These findings offer important information for understanding tumor heterogeneity in breast cancer and developing new therapeutic strategies. The potential role of polyamine metabolism in breast cancer was a significant discovery in this study. In the tumor microenvironment, polyamine was able to be aberrantly activated and this activation of polyamines in cancers is associated with poor prognoses including breast cancer. These findings indicate a potential ployamine metabolism related pathway in breast cancer that may be used for treatment purposes. Our studies provided potential use of polyamine metabolism inhibitors in treating breast cancer and independent future investigations could be undertaken to confirm if Polyamines are important during different aspect of tumor growth.

We also compared risk scores and functions of immune cells with the high-risk group for Armario's cohort. These observations supported a conclusion that risk scores might affect the expression and function of immune cells, thereby modulating tumor responses to immunotherapy. It is the discovery that theoretically paves the way for personalised treatment strategies to be employed in accordance with immune cell status.

The application of machine learning in cancer research, particularly in the analysis of single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA seq) data, has become an important tool for revealing the complexity and heterogeneity of the tumor microenvironment (TME). Deep learning models have been used to characterize tumor heterogeneity, including morphological diversity, which is caused by cellular heterogeneity and reflects the complex dynamics of tumor proliferation and metastasis. Machine learning models can identify gene expression patterns related to tumor proliferation and immune cell infiltration from scRNA seq data, providing potential biomarkers for cancer treatment. By applying machine learning to scRNA seq data, it is possible to predict the effects of specific drugs on tumor cells [ 33 – 35 ].

Our machine learning models for breast cancer prediction were quite successful, which may help improve several important aspects of clinical decision-making. This level of predictive performance and generalisability suggest that these models could be important tools to aid in breast cancer diagnosis and assessing treatment response. The superior performance of this model to deep learning models commonly used by radiologists in practice makes it clear that more research will need to be done on such algorithms and their potential use cases across additional tumor types.
sections.conclusion: The present study Seurat and machine learning model has uncovered novel immune cell infiltration, gene co-expression status in the microenvironment of breast cancer via full single-cell analysis.
